title: Rujuta Diwekar's Three Forgotten Summer Coolants That Need No Electricity or AC
excerpt: Celebrity nutritionist recommends vetiver-infused water, mehendi, and buttermilk as traditional Indian solutions to beat the summer heat without modern appliances.
body:
• Rujuta Diwekar recommends vetiver (vala) water, mehendi application, and buttermilk as three forgotten Indian coolants that require no electricity or air conditioning
  • Buttermilk serves as a natural prebiotic, probiotic, and postbiotic while fixing electrolyte imbalance caused by dehydration and heat exhaustion
  • Medical experts endorse these traditional practices but caution they should complement — not replace — standard medical precautions during extreme heat

Celebrity nutritionist Rujuta Diwekar has shared three traditional Indian remedies she relies on every summer to stay cool — none of which require electricity or air conditioning.

"3 forgotten coolants for which you require neither electricity nor AC," Diwekar wrote on Instagram, adding that the trio will keep "your body, brain and gut calm" through India's punishing summer months.

Vetiver: India's Original Infused Water

Diwekar's first recommendation is vala roots, commonly known as vetiver or khus. Calling it "India's OG infused water," she suggests placing a few strands in a vessel of water and drinking it throughout the day. Vetiver has long been used in Indian households as a natural coolant, and the fragrant roots contain antibacterial and antimicrobial compounds that research suggests may also help combat skin conditions, according to Dr Ranjan Modi, Senior Consultant in Interventional Cardiology at Medanta, Noida.

Mehendi: More Than a Wedding Tradition

The second suggestion may surprise many — applying mehendi (henna) on the hands. Diwekar describes it as a "particularly calming activity during the hotter months," noting that the fragrance of henna helps the body and mind settle down. The practice of applying henna during summer is rooted in centuries of Ayurvedic tradition, where henna paste is believed to have natural cooling properties that lower body temperature through the palms.

Buttermilk: The Everyday Powerhouse

Diwekar's third and most emphatic recommendation is buttermilk, consumed two to three times daily. "It has protein, calcium, and B12," she explained. "It also works as a prebiotic, probiotic and postbiotic — but most importantly, it helps in fixing electrolyte imbalance due to dehydration and heat exhaustion."

This aligns with longstanding nutritional science. Buttermilk — known as chaas, mattha, or majjiga across different Indian regions — is a fermented dairy drink that replenishes sodium, potassium, and other minerals lost through perspiration, making it a natural oral rehydration solution.

What Medical Experts Say

Dr Modi confirmed that traditional Indian summer practices carry genuine health benefits. "Indians adopted several traditional practices during summer to ensure their wellness," he said. "These habits include adequate hydration, proper nutrition, and eating seasonal foods, which contribute to the body's ability to adapt better to hot weather conditions."

He recommends a broader arsenal of traditional coolants, including yoghurt, coconut water, seasonal fruits, and lighter home-cooked meals, all of which assist in hydration and minimise the risk of heatstroke.

However, Dr Modi cautioned that these lifestyle strategies "should not replace necessary medical precautions in times of extremely hot weather conditions." He warned that diabetics, hypertensive patients, and people with renal or cardiovascular conditions should be "particularly careful" and watch for signs of heat exhaustion such as dizziness, nausea, and disorientation.

A Broader Push for Change

Diwekar also used her post to advocate for systemic action. "The need of the hour is for our policy makers to step in and protect our homes from getting overheated," she wrote in her Instagram caption, pointing to the growing need for urban planning and building design that reduces indoor heat without relying solely on energy-intensive cooling systems.

Her recommendations come as India continues to grapple with increasingly severe heat waves, with temperatures in several northern states exceeding 45°C in recent summers. Traditional cooling practices, once considered outdated by urban Indians, are experiencing a revival as people seek affordable, sustainable alternatives to air conditioning.
